01-reality-of-ownership.title: The costs, on paper.
01-reality-of-ownership.standfirst: A one-page reference to keep alongside any acquisition conversation. The items below are what to have in writing before signing.
01-reality-of-ownership.intent: Write down the expected costs before the first acquisition conversation. The numbers do not need to be perfect, but they need to be in writing.

items.question: An annual operating-cost projection in writing, with each line named (crew salary, insurance, berths, fuel, refit reserve, compliance, contingency).
items.detail: Use a line-by-line projection rather than a single-figure estimate.

items.question: The projection benchmarked against named published sources (YPI Crew, Quay Crew, Pantaenius, MYBA).
items.detail: Each of those publishes data that can be cited rather than inferred from a conversation.

items.question: The running cost calculator on this site, run with the buyer’s own size, type, region, and intensity.
items.detail: Source assumptions are named on every line.

items.question: A depreciation projection across the intended hold period, against broker-aggregated data.
items.detail: Yatco and IYC publish broker-aggregated rates; Yacht Hunter argues against fixed schedules.

items.question: An estimate of the number of weeks per year the yacht will be used.
items.detail: Below 12 weeks of intended use, charter and fractional access cover the same calendar at lower fixed cost.

items.question: An intended hold horizon of seven years or more.
items.detail: Over a shorter hold, the steep early years of depreciation make up a larger share of the total cost.

items.question: The use case tested against the buyer’s calendar, household, and family availability for the next five years.
items.detail: Chapter 9’s case puts owner attention on a 49 m yacht at 40 to 60 days a year.

items.question: If charter has been proposed as an offset to ownership cost, a worked case based on yacht size, weekly rate, and weeks.
items.detail: BOAT International publishes case studies of charter income against running cost.

items.question: A decision, made in advance, on whether the prime-season weeks (mid-July to mid-August in the Med, December to early January in the Caribbean) are available for charter.
items.detail: The published case-study yields depend on charter income from those weeks.

items.question: The charter projection checked against the published case studies, including those that broke even or made a loss, and the exception.
A conversation, with someone whose income is not contingent on the deal, about the case for not buying.
items.detail: Parties paid contingent on a sale do not raise this.

items.question: A maximum total cost of ownership across years one to three that the buyer is comfortable absorbing, written down.
An option to delay the acquisition by six months if any of the items above remain uncertain.

02-reading-the-market.title: Checking a listing before making an offer.
02-reading-the-market.standfirst: Twelve items to keep alongside any shortlist conversation. The items below are drawn from the data published on listing portals and in the BOAT International Global Order Book.
02-reading-the-market.intent: Days-on-market and price-reduction history are public on the listing portals. The items below are what to look at before the first broker conversation.

items.question: Days-on-market, from the listing’s original entry, on the broker portal.
items.detail: Compare against the most recent published days-on-market median for the size band, and note its date.

items.question: Price-reduction history by date and amount.
items.detail: Reduction history is published on the listing portal alongside days-on-market.

items.question: Three comparable hulls (size, age, yard tier, propulsion) currently on market, with their asking, days, and reductions.
How many comparable yachts are for sale or on order, from the brokerage listings for yachts over 30 m and the BOAT International Global Order Book.
If new build is also under consideration: slot availability at the relevant yard tier (Lürssen, Feadship, Oceanco, Heesen, Sanlorenzo).
How far US buying, encouraged by the 100 percent depreciation allowance in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is affecting prices in the relevant size band.
items.detail: It varies by segment rather than across the whole market. The independent adviser can speak to it for the specific hull.

items.question: Broker phrases such as “about to offer”, “about to move” and “tightening” noted as claims to be checked, not market evidence.
A note, in writing, of any introductions the broker is offering (surveyor, lawyer, captain, management company), and the relationships behind them.
items.detail: Firms introduced by a brokerage may pay it referral fees. The disclosure is asked for, not always volunteered.

items.question: The comparable scan, in writing, with named comparables and the reasoning behind each.
A ceiling price, agreed in advance and in writing, above which the buyer will walk away.
The comparable scan run independently of the listing broker, through the buyer’s own adviser.
Two further candidates on the shortlist, in case this hull does not close.
items.detail: A buyer with only one candidate is under more pressure to accept the seller’s terms; a buyer with alternatives can walk away.

03-how-the-industry-works.title: Disclosures worth having in writing.
03-how-the-industry-works.standfirst: Questions to ask any party introduced into the acquisition about who pays them and who owns them.
03-how-the-industry-works.intent: When a brokerage offers buyer support without a fee, the work is still paid for, by the seller’s commission or by referral fees from suppliers. The items below set out what to ask.

items.question: The commission scale being applied (IYBA flat 10 percent, MYBA sliding scale), and the resulting fee.
Any dual agency on the transaction, documented in writing beyond the standard form clause.
The brokerage’s ownership structure (PE-backed, public-parent, founder-led, yard-tied).
items.detail: Each kind of owner gives the brokerage different incentives.

items.question: For each party the brokerage has introduced (lawyer, surveyor, management company, paint specialist, insurance broker, recruitment agency): the referral or retrocession arrangement, if any, and at what rate.
Written disclosure of every referral relationship and retrocession arrangement on every introduction.
items.detail: Referral fees are legal only if disclosed (OnboardOnline legal column).

items.question: If disclosure is declined, an independent adviser engaged to identify and document the relationships.
items.detail: This can be part of an independent adviser’s scope.

items.question: The candidate’s introduction route (broker, seller, or independent agency engaged by the buyer).
Any prior commercial relationships with brokers, yards, suppliers, or management companies that might continue into employment.
The captain’s pay structure (straight salary, or any bonus, charter share, or referral-related elements).
An understanding of which parties in the transaction would walk away from a deal that did not benefit the buyer.
items.detail: An independent adviser paid only by the buyer has no financial reason to want the deal to close.

items.question: At least one party in the transaction whose income does not depend on the deal closing.

04-acquisition-process.title: Fifteen items to complete before closing.
04-acquisition-process.standfirst: A reference list across the 12 to 24 week acquisition window. Most of the work comes well before closing.
04-acquisition-process.intent: The contract terms are fixed at closing, and most of the work that determines them is done in the first ten weeks. Complete the items below in that period.

items.question: A shortlist drawn from at least two brokerages, plus an independent off-market scan.
Budget figure kept with the independent adviser; brokers briefed on use case, size band and propulsion.
items.detail: Brokers are usually paid from the seller’s commission, which rises with the price. Disclosure tells you how they are paid; it does not change that.

items.question: Shortlisted yachts walked in the company of the independent adviser as well as the broker.
An independently engaged surveyor, with no relationship to the broker.
items.detail: Ward & McKenzie and Patton Marine are recognised firms.

items.question: Survey scope sufficient for the yacht (4 to 7 days afloat plus haul-out, USD 25 to 60 k, full mechanical and electrical, paint specialist, class society inspector).
A renegotiation, on every material deficiency the survey finds.
items.detail: Renegotiation on material survey deficiencies is standard practice.

items.question: The buyer’s own captain candidate, surveyor, and (where relevant) chief engineer present.
Trial scope covering the failure modes the survey identified, plus stability, vibration, noise, and electronics under representative load.
Readiness to renegotiate or walk away if the trial reveals issues, rather than closing on schedule.
A separate written legal opinion from independent counsel on the VAT structure.
items.detail: Hill Dickinson, WFW, Ince, Stephenson Harwood, Reed Smith are recognised firms.

items.question: Flag-state choice analysed against owner residence, cruising area, charter intent, financing, and family-office structuring.
Projected annual tax, structuring and flag cost (EUR 50 to 150 k on a 40 m yacht) included in the budget, with flag and class fees counted once against the chapter 7 operating figure.

A contract with clean title warranties, an inventory matching the sale, agreed deficiencies remediated or priced, an acceptance protocol with adequate time, and a governing law clause that is not the seller’s home jurisdiction.
A 3 to 5 day technical handover with the seller’s captain, the buyer’s captain, and the chief engineer.
A closing date the buyer will not bring forward under pressure.
items.detail: An early close suits the seller and the parties paid on completion; the buyer carries what was not checked.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.title: What to settle, before signing the new build contract.
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.standfirst: Three threshold tests for new build. Ten contract points to settle at heads of terms. The items below are what specialist counsel walks through.
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.intent: The items below are the points specialist counsel and the owner’s representative settle at heads of terms.

items.question: A hold horizon of seven to ten years, on paper.
items.detail: Below seven years, the new build cost premium does not amortise.

items.question: A use that no brokerage yacht meets, in size, layout, propulsion, range or operation.

Commitment to four things: independent owner’s representative engaged before contract, specialist shipbuilding counsel, technical due diligence on the yard’s order book and financial condition, and willingness to push back on the yard’s first-draft contract.

groups.heading: Contract drafting at heads of terms

items.question: Stage payment loading reviewed: commercial shipbuilding puts 40 percent or more before delivery; custom yacht contracts often well over half.
items.detail: The more is paid before delivery, the more depends on the refund guarantee and on independent checks of each milestone.

items.question: No stage payment released without independent verification of the milestone behind it.
items.detail: Yard-standard milestones are often self-certified by the yard.

items.question: Refund guarantee from a bank of high credit standing, independent of the yard and its group, payable on demand, covering all instalments with interest, and valid to delivery plus a margin.
items.detail: It repays only sums paid, not lost use, financing costs, or owner-supplied items, and only against a valid termination and a correctly presented demand.

items.question: Refund guarantee expiry diarised against the contract’s long-stop date, and the guarantor’s written consent obtained for every material variation.
items.detail: Builds run late and variations are frequent. A guarantee that has lapsed or been voided is usually discovered only when the buyer calls it.

items.question: Rights to the yard’s financial information at set intervals, to suspend payments on named warning signs, and to step in and complete the vessel elsewhere.
items.detail: Warning signs include missed supplier payments, a rating downgrade, a covenant breach, or a shareholder change. Step-in covers the unfinished hull, materials, and design files.

items.question: Liquidated damages cap defined and at a level that reflects the project.
items.detail: Industry typical: 1 percent of contract value per week of delay, capped at 5 to 10 percent.

items.question: Force majeure burden on the yard to prove “but for” causation, per English law.
Change order procedure with pre-agreed unit rates and third-party quote rights for variations above a defined threshold.
items.detail: Without this, the yard prices variations at its discretion.

items.question: Defect notification deadlines understood, with the consequences of late notification clear.
Warranty length negotiated (12 months standard, 24 months achievable).
Cancellation thresholds (150 days post-delivery / 180 days total) understood and within the project’s tolerance.
Title during construction agreed (yard-retained until delivery, or progressive transfer).
items.detail: Where title passes progressively: hull and materials marked and kept separately, inspection rights, insurance with the buyer named, a right of entry and removal on default, and a local-law opinion that the transfer will be recognised. Where the yard keeps title, the refund guarantee is the main protection.

items.question: Title or security registered in the form the build country recognises.
items.detail: Title follows the law of the build country, whatever the contract says. In Italy, that means transcription in the register of vessels under construction.

items.question: Dispute forum on English law plus LMAA arbitration, the practitioner default.
Owner’s representative paid by the buyer, with any commission from the yard, a broker or a supplier disclosed in writing, with its amount and payer, before engagement.
Fee structure shown in writing before contract signature.
Representative present on site weekly through the build, with quantified snag list reporting against original scope.

06-refit.title: What to settle before the refit contract, or the sale.
06-refit.standfirst: For the refit, and for the sale if that is the better course.
06-refit.intent: The 30 percent threshold is a practitioner rule of thumb. Most items limit overrun; the last group prepares for a sale.

items.question: Projected refit cost as a percentage of pre-refit market value, compared with the cost of selling and buying a replacement.
items.detail: Above 30 percent, consider selling.

items.question: A ten-year cost forecast with four budgets kept apart: maintenance, planned refit, regulatory works, owner upgrades.
The yard’s physical limits checked first: lift capacity and beam, shed, air draft, approach depth.
Yard chosen for this scope and tonnage on track record and project team, not cheapest quote.
Yard slot booked as far ahead as the yard’s order book: up to 24 months at top European yards.
At a service yard, one coordinator appointed in writing, and every trade contract on the same law and forum.
Scope defined in writing (deliverables, materials, finishes) and reviewed line by line.
A pre-works survey recorded as the baseline for emergent work, with critical areas opened first.
Work sorted into mandatory, recommended, and the owner’s call, with a Deferred Items Register for what is not done.
A design freeze date, after which every change is a priced variation signed by a named person for the owner.
Long-lead items given decide-by dates, and the contract type (fixed price, cost plus, target cost) matched to the scope.
A naval architect’s tonnage check where work adds enclosed volume (over 1 percent on 499 GT triggers remeasurement).
A contingency of 10 to 25 percent, by how far the hull has been opened before.
Payments tied to defined deliverables rather than calendar dates, with a retention held against snag close-out.
The yard’s lien and the terms for release against security (escrow or bank guarantee) agreed before haul-out.
Redelivery defined in the contract: snags, sea trial criteria, warranty, as-built drawings, spares, class papers, final account.
VAT structure selected by independent counsel, with any Spanish IPR authorisation in place before works begin.
A dated photo and video condition record before yard entry, and a recorded captain handover in the first fortnight.
Owner’s representative on site at least weekly, with photographic snag list and variance against budget.
Builder’s risk wording read in full: owner co-insured, waiver of subrogation, whole-vessel sum insured, hot work and transit covered.
Listing agreement read by the seller’s own lawyer: term, marketing commitment, commission after it ends, governing law.
Commission scale, any split with a buyer’s broker, and any dual agency set out in writing.
Records, class status and VAT evidence ready; asking price set against published days on market.
Seller’s warranties and any guarantee agreed with a cap and an expiry date.

07-operations.title: Five operating decisions, in year one.
07-operations.standfirst: Five decisions whose effects last for as long as the yacht is owned. The list below is what to set up in year one and revisit annually.
07-operations.intent: The captain hire affects the other four decisions for as long as the yacht is owned. The items below are what to set up in year one.

items.question: At least five captain candidates, all sourced through routes outside the broker’s relationship.
Evidence from interview that the candidate will question the owner’s plans on itinerary, maintenance, budget and crew where needed.
Disclosure of the captain’s prior commercial relationships with brokers, yards, suppliers, or management companies that might continue into employment.
Management company introduced by the independent adviser, not by the broker.
Written disclosure of any referral fees or commissions from suppliers (paint, refit yards, insurance, recruitment).
Contract terms that protect the buyer’s interests in flag-state interactions, ISM and MLC compliance where they apply, and audits.

Competitive quotes from at least three brokers with over-30 m yacht experience (the chapter names Howden, Pantaenius, AON Marine, Gallagher Specialty, Marsh and PIB Marine), each with its commission disclosed in writing.
Hull premium within the practitioner range of 0.7 to 1.5 percent of insured value (well-maintained 40 to 50 m), with a reason given for any figure outside it.
P&I cover (crew injury, environmental, third-party, charter guest claims) at USD 500 m third-party limit through Shipowners’ Club or Steamship Mutual.
Private operation across years one to three, with a decision in year four whether to introduce charter.
items.detail: Practitioners usually wait until year four before converting a privately operated yacht to charter, by which time the owner has three years of actual use to go on.

items.question: If charter is being considered from year one, a worked case based on yacht size, weekly rate, and weeks against the BOAT International published cases (chapter 1).
A clear decision on whether to release prime-season weeks, given that charter income does not cover the cost of ownership for the median operator.
A refit reserve from year one, sized at 5 to 15 percent of insured hull value across the five-year cycle.
The reserve checked against the 30 to 50 percent by which refits commonly overrun their quotes.
An annual capex plan revisited with the captain and owner’s representative present.

08-motor-versus-sail.title: Running the comparison, before defaulting to motor.
08-motor-versus-sail.standfirst: A reference for the buyer at the point of choosing between motor, sailing yacht, and hybrid drive.
08-motor-versus-sail.intent: First-time buyers commonly default to motor. The items below are what the comparison depends on.

items.question: A realistic view of the cruising calendar. Are the buyer’s seasons fixed-date and inflexible, or is there room to wait 36 to 60 hours for suitable weather before a transatlantic crossing?
items.detail: Fixed-schedule cruising favours motor or hybrid. A flexible season opens the sailing yacht and hybrid options.

items.question: A view on how much the yacht’s carbon emissions matter, given the principal’s family office, foundation or public role.
items.detail: Sailing yachts and hybrid yachts emit less carbon than conventional motor yachts.

items.question: The seven-year arithmetic, run on paper, across capex, opex, depreciation, and residual.
items.detail: On the chapter’s 35 m figures, a quality sailing yacht comes in about a fifth to a third below the equivalent motor programme on total seven-year cost, and 25 to 40 percent below where it holds its value better.

groups.heading: Operating cost comparison, on a 50 m

items.question: Annual fuel projection, sailing yacht against motor. EUR 60 to 120 k for the sailing yacht, EUR 200 to 350 k for the motor at 400 cruising hours.
Crew complement and pay, sailing yacht against motor. 9 to 12 crew on a 50 m sailing yacht, 12 to 16 on a comparable motor.

Maintenance: rigging and sail wardrobe reserves on the sailing yacht set against engine wear and stabiliser systems on the motor. Net annual maintenance is broadly comparable, but more of the sailing yacht’s comes as large sums at long intervals.
Total annual operating cost. Sailing yacht typically 70 to 85 percent of the motor figure on equivalent length and use.
EU ETS Maritime exposure. The system applies only to ships of 5,000 GT and above used for commercial passenger or cargo transport; a privately used yacht is outside it at any size.
items.detail: Confirm the yacht’s GT, commercial or private status and passenger certification with the flag and the yacht lawyer. A July 2026 Commission proposal to extend the system below 5,000 GT does not name yachts.

items.question: HVO availability at the buyer’s home cruising port. HVO is a drop-in diesel replacement with lifecycle emissions up to about 90 percent lower, by feedstock; supply is strongest in the Mediterranean.

If new build, the emission control areas the yacht will cruise and the NOx Tier III dates that apply there, whether the engine maker approves HVO, and any methanol-ready or fuel-cell specification. Available from the larger Northern European yards on request.
Whether hybrid drive (Heesen FDHF, Sanlorenzo SX, and equivalent programmes) has been priced into the comparison alongside motor and sailing yacht.
items.detail: Hybrid drive costs less to run and emits less carbon than a conventional motor yacht, but more than a sailing yacht.

items.question: Battery hotel-load capability on the relevant new build candidates, with the capacity in kWh and the hours of silent running it supports.
A written summary of the comparison, signed off by the buyer and the independent adviser before any broker engagement on the chosen path.
Written acceptance of the expected resale value of whichever type of yacht is chosen.

09-decision-framework.title: The ten questions, applied to every adviser.
09-decision-framework.standfirst: The ten questions are designed to be put to anyone proposing to advise on the acquisition, including the publisher of The First Owner’s Reference. The publisher’s own answers are on the colophon.
09-decision-framework.intent: The questions below test whether an adviser’s interests match the buyer’s, by establishing who pays them. They are designed to be put to people, not to be answered alone.

items.question: Who introduced the yacht (or yard) to me, and who pays them?
Who recommended the lawyer, and who pays them?
Who recommended the surveyor, and who pays them?
Who recommended the management company, and who pays them?
Has any party offered to provide their services “at no cost,” and if so, who is paying them?
Has every party I am working with disclosed their commercial relationships in writing, including referral fees, retrocessions, and equity holdings in counterparties?
Is my legal counsel independent of the broker, the yard, and the management company, and is their fee paid by me directly?
Is my surveyor independent of the seller and of the broker, and is their fee paid by me directly?
If I am building, is my owner’s representative paid by me, and has any contingent fee, yard commission or referral relationship been disclosed to me in writing?
If I asked any of these parties to walk away from a deal that would not benefit me, would they?
items.detail: If the answer is no for any party, its interest in the deal closing may outweigh the buyer’s.

groups.heading: Before setting up the ownership structure

items.question: Will the yacht be for private enjoyment only, or is charter a possibility, even if not immediately?
Where will the yacht primarily operate and cruise?
Will finance be involved?
Will ownership rest with one individual, or involve family, succession, or more than one beneficial owner?
How and where will the yacht be imported, and what will its VAT position be?
items.detail: Develop the ownership structure, VAT position, and importation strategy together, before contracts are exchanged, not as separate decisions afterwards. Getting the sequence wrong exposes the owner to VAT liabilities and penalties calculated on the value of the yacht.
